posts.title: The Dutch Design Awards 2019 named eight winners at a private night in June, then let 5,000 visitors choose a greenhouse that had not won its category
posts.subtitle: The 2019 awards read through the organizer's updates, entry pages and winner portraits, the festival's releases, press reports and the official photo archive
posts.seoTitle: Dutch Design Awards 2019: eight winners and a public vote
posts.description: How the 2019 Dutch Design Awards chose eight winners in June, what the committees and jury wrote, and why a greenhouse that had only been nominated won the public vote in October.

r: The Dutch Design Awards of 2019 announced their eight winners at a private night in June and then let more than 5,000 visitors choose a favorite in October, and the visitors chose a greenhouse that had been nominated but had not won its category.

I like an award that can be checked against its own paperwork. This essay reads the 2019 awards from public sources only: the organizer's updates, entry pages and winner portraits, the festival's releases, press reports and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive. It reports no visit and no interview, and where sources disagree it says which one settled the question.

blocks.x: The rules for 2019

r: The organizer's 2019 rules, in Dutch, set the frame. Work had to be produced, realized, presented or published between May 1, 2018 and May 1, 2019.
Experts scouted from March 1 to 22, and designers could enter themselves from March 1 to April 17.
Entry cost 75 euros plus VAT for the six main categories and 150 euros plus VAT for Best Commissioning.
The four criteria are impact, distinctive character, expressiveness and production method.
The rules say the Public Award goes to the winner with the most public votes, cast during Dutch Design Week on winners from the categories.

blocks.x: A private night in June, a public hall in October

r: The nominees were announced in May. Independent committees of design experts nominated three projects in each of eight categories: Product, Habitat, Communication, Fashion, Design Research, Service & Systems, Best Commissioning and Young Designer.
The winners were named on Wednesday evening, June 12, 2019, at what the organizer calls a private, festive Award Night, where the BNO Piet Zwart Prize was also presented.
The organizer's winners update explains the machinery. In total 36 committee members chose the three nominations per category from all submitted and scouted projects.
They judged on impact, distinctive character, expressiveness and method of production, plus a few criteria specific to a category.
The eight committee chairs together formed the jury that chose the winners, led by jury chair Ine Frings.
The chairs were Angelique Spaninks, Bert Hagendoorn, JaapJan Berg, Joost Alferink, Liesbeth In 't Hout, Pieter Aarts, Roosje Klap and Saskia van Stein.
The 2016 and 2017 announcements describe a different split, with a committee shortlisting and an international professional jury choosing the winners.

The same update gives the Young Designer money: winner Simone Post received a Keep an Eye Young Designer Grant of 12,000 euros, and the two other nominees, Amber Jae Slooten and Ninamounah, 9,000 euros each.
The Keep an Eye announcement from May repeats the amounts and quotes Olivier van Herpt, the 2018 winner, on using the money to industrialize his ceramic 3D printing.
The winners, the update says, give shape to the philosophy of less, but better.
The festival's own item lists the eight in category order and gives the exhibition dates as October 19 to 27, 2019, with a public vote for the Public Award.
That exhibition was a nine-day overview on the third floor of VEEM, the organizer says, and the later Public Award update credits its design to Studio Daphna Laurens and George&Harrison.
The festival that surrounded it drew 350,000 visitors, 5,000 fewer than the record year of 2018, according to IO+, under the theme If not now, then when?

blocks.x: The eight winners

r: Communication went to RNDR for OPENRNDR, an open source framework for creative coding.
The committee called it an innovative, open, cross-media platform that heralds a revolution for the profession, built to support the design community.

In the winner portrait the co-founder Edwin Jakobs explains the position: knowledge was shared in the early years of software design, then shut away once software became profitable, and OPENRNDR documents its own framework in plain handbooks so designers can use and extend it.

Design Research went to RE-source by Ester van de Wiel, Joost Adriaanse, David Hamers and Ginette Verstraete, a research project that maps urban residual flows in Rotterdam as a resource for circular thinking.
The committee called it collaboration at the highest level and thorough design research.

The makers' portrait adds that five Design Academy Eindhoven alumni worked with five residual streams: Jos Klarenbeek on concrete paving stones, Thom Bindels on silt, Simone Post on grass, Paul Slot on street furniture and Manon van Hoeckel on plant material.
Post and Van Hoeckel are both Young Designer winners, in 2019 and 2018.
Fashion went to Bonne Reijn for De Rrusie Suit, made with Kevin De Rrusie Lucas, the second of his self-described poor man's suits.
The committee read it as a response to style saturation in a fashion landscape where luxury is democratized, the power of uniformity.
In the portrait Reijn says the brand produces only on demand and shows its own friends on the sidewalk in front of his house.
Habitat went to the LocHal in Tilburg by Civic Architects, Braaksma & Roos Architectenbureau, Inside Outside with Petra Blaisse, and Mecanoo for the interior.

The entry calls the former locomotive workshop the new beating heart of the Spoorzone, a public city hall with a library concept, work and meeting rooms, a city kitchen and two art installations; the commissioning party was the municipality of Tilburg.
The committee valued the respect for the old building combined with a new program.
In the portrait, Ingrid van der Heijden of Civic Architects says the interior was designed to be reversible, so that in theory it could be removed in fifty years to give back the old building.

Product went to the Gispen Sett CE, a sofa designed by Peter van de Water and made from 95 percent recycled materials, with a printed body developed with TU Delft, Searious Business and 10XL from the company's own plastic waste.
The committee praised 3D printing at furniture scale for consumer production.
Service & Systems went to CLEVER°FRANKE for the BMX Live Visualisation, a real-time data visualization for the Royal Dutch Cycling Union that helps riders analyze runs and judges assess them.
Gert Franke says in the portrait that the challenge was to track a dynamic sport in three dimensions and make it understandable live for a large audience.
The entry describes the sport's Olympic debut as 2020.
The firm returned in 2023 as a Data & Interaction winner for Voices from the Frontlines.

Best Commissioning went to the municipality of Amsterdam for the Puccinimethode, the design system for the city's public space: roads, squares, parks and gardens, with profiles, materials and details.
The committee said that because the local authority prioritizes quality, it defines the right framework for careful commissioning.

The project lead Heiko Miskotte says the name came in 2001, when civil servants bought bonbons at Chocolatier Puccini and one said that if the quality of Amsterdam's public space became as good as the bonbons they would have reached their goal.

Young Designer went to Simone Post, a Design Academy Eindhoven graduate who works on the visible reuse of materials and has made clothing from recycled sneakers for Adidas, a book for the plastic recycler ECO-oh! and a carpet for Vlisco.
The committee praised an aesthetic that goes beyond the typical look of recycling.
The portrait quotes her on looking for products that can scale, not only statements about reuse.

The BNO Piet Zwart Prize went to the spatial designer Frans Bevers of the firm OPERA, who was recognized for his contribution to exhibition design; the prize was presented by Timo de Rijk, chair of its jury, at the June 12 night.

blocks.x: The public chose a nominee

r: Power Plant by Marjan van Aubel Studio won the Public Award, the festival says, in what it calls a neck-and-neck race with Simone Post and with Gispen.
The organizer's update puts the turnout at more than 5,000 visitors in VEEM.
Power Plant is an energy-neutral greenhouse that produces both electricity and food from sunlight; Van Aubel calls the approach Solar Democracy.
The archive lists Power Plant as a Design Research nominee, not a winner.
The winner in that category was RE-source.
The committee wrote of Power Plant that it is immediately an icon for the use of solar energy and food production.
The organizer's pre-vote update says the independent committee chose 8 winners from the 24 nominees, and that visitors could vote for one of those 8.
The result contradicts that: a nominee won, and the results update describes the exhibition as showing all 24 projects.

I follow the result and read the pre-vote line as loose wording. The award announcement was set for the evening at Cafe CMYK, the bar on the Ketelhuisplein, with votes counted between 18:00 and 19:00.

blocks.x: What the jury report said

r: The organizer's jury report, published as an appendix to the winners release, names four themes. Applicable: circularity now often serves as a condition for a commission, and creating awareness is no longer enough. Design integrates in organizations: public and business commissioners increasingly build design and creative thinking into their organizations. Sober and accessible: winning designers radically choose to design for everyone. New design aesthetic: designers formulate, develop and produce the tools and methods they need.
It closes on a contagious kind of optimism, with developing and collaborating done with enjoyment and generosity.

The jury's own paragraphs differ from the committee paragraphs on the entry pages, and where they differ they sharpen. On the Sett CE the jury wrote that this is a glimpse of the new aesthetic norm in circular design, which does not scream sustainability, with reuse quietly built into a timeless design.
On De Rrusie Suit it called the statement radical in its simplicity, the uniform as a sober and democratic canvas for identity.
On the LocHal it noted that it is admirable that such a relatively young agency tackled the task so energetically.
On the Puccinimethode it said the public sector shows how to take control within complex procurement.
On Simone Post it said the jury curiously awaits her next steps.

blocks.x: What the committees and chairs said they were looking for

r: The committee texts for the winners share a vocabulary. The OPENRNDR committee wrote about a revolution for the profession, the RE-source committee about complexity approached with playfulness, the Sett CE committee about an example for the entire manufacturing industry, and the Puccinimethode committee about a careful, almost artisanal method that lies hidden beneath the surface.
The Young Designer committee said Simone Post's language transcends the typical aesthetic of recycling and upcycling.

The chairs wrote their own short columns in the months around the night. Angelique Spaninks, chair for Design Research, noted that the category had been added only about five years earlier and asked whether it means research on, through or by design, concluding that the open, combined approach seems the most fruitful.
Liesbeth In 't Hout asked why it is harder to judge a designer's collection than separate products.
JaapJan Berg described being asked at the award night what Habitat means and answering, unsatisfactorily, that it is practically everything.
Pieter Aarts, chair for Best Commissioning, wrote about a world growing more complex through digitalization, fake news and e-commerce.

Joost Alferink's column states what he sees as the awards' purpose beyond celebration: what happens in the field, how it connects to social debate and how to involve a wider public, while admitting that judging sustainability, repairability and reuse takes more than one jury session and years for effects to show.
The organizer announced the series of eight columns under one heading.

blocks.x: The nominees who did not win

r: In Communication, Richard Niessen's Palace of Typographic Masonry, an imaginary institute for graphic design, was a nominee for the second time after 2017, and The Rodina's identity for the Sonic Acts festival theme HEREAFTER was the third nominee.
In Design Research, Martina Huynh's Basic Income Café let visitors experience two basic income economies through coffee.
Huynh won the Young Designer Award in 2022 with Jonas Althaus for Cream on Chrome.
In Fashion, Ninamounah's Collection 004 Evolve Around Me and MAISON the FAUX's MAISON pour MAISON were the other finalists.
Ninamounah also stood as a Young Designer finalist, so she appears under both Fashion and Young Designer in the archive.
She won Fashion in 2020 for Collection 005.

In Habitat, Ector Hoogstad Architecten's bicycle parking facility near Utrecht station holds space for 12,500 bikes, and the Werkwarenhuis in 's-Hertogenbosch turned a former animal feed factory into a concept store and halfway house for people distanced from the labor market.
In Product, Lex Pott's Poplars reinterpreted wooden clogs and UNStudio's The Coolest White is a coating that reflects sunlight on buildings.

In Service & Systems, Fabrique and Q42's Below The Surface made archaeological finds from the North/South metro line accessible, and Moooi's The Button gave design objects a digital proof of authenticity.
In Best Commissioning, MOJO's Lowlands artwork and website with Hansje van Halem and Fabrique, and Interpolis with Freshheads, were the other finalists.
The Lowlands entry is a sequel to the 2018 win.
In Young Designer, Amber Jae Slooten fused fashion with animation.

blocks.x: After the awards

r: The LocHal won again. The World Architecture Festival named it Building of the Year 2019, with the prize presented in Amsterdam on December 6, among more than a thousand entries, the organizer reports.
The update recalls that the 1932 locomotive hall, used for repairs until 2010, had seemed destined for demolition a few years earlier.

A guest column by Nolan Giles, written from outside the jury room, makes a point the entry texts do not. Giles writes that the Young Designer committee, represented by Saskia van Stein, had questioned whether Simone Post's pieces look recycled at all, and concludes that Dutch designers can now put beauty on the agenda.

blocks.x: What the exhibition photographs add

r: The album of 62 photographs, which I read on October 9, 2026 and did not reopen for this version, shows a long concrete hall with yellow pillars and banners hung from the pillars, each category named on a banner.
Black frames hold dark boards with project texts in Dutch and English, each ending with a jury line.
A colophon banner lists the committees and jury with Ine Frings first as chairman, which matches the organizer's winners update.
The Young Designer corner shows a board headed Winner Simone Post and a round striped rug of recycled sneaker rubber, and a hanging banner names the winner and both nominees.
The photographs do not say who designed the setting. The organizer's Public Award update names Studio Daphna Laurens and George&Harrison.

blocks.x: Where 2019 sits in the archive, and elsewhere in the festival

r: The organizer's archive lists 24 entries for 2019, the second year at that size.
The count is mine, from the listing.
CLEVER°FRANKE is the clearest repeat visitor in the 2019 list: a 2013 nominee, a 2015 nominee, a 2019 winner and later a 2021 and 2023 winner.
Gemeente Amsterdam had been a nominee in 2003 and 2009 before the Puccinimethode won.
Gispen had been a Best Commissioning nominee in 2013.
Ben van Berkel and UNStudio appear in 2008 and 2009 for architecture before The Coolest White.
Hansje van Halem's Lowlands work was a 2018 winner and a 2019 nominee.

The organizer also pointed visitors to winners' work elsewhere in the festival. CLEVER°FRANKE showed Aiml, a project about how artificial intelligence and machine learning work, in hall three of the Klokgebouw.
Gispen showed the Sett CE sofa in the Embassy of Sustainable Design, and RNDR was part of the festival's Digital Route.

blocks.x: What the winners did next

r: The organizer reported on several 2019 names afterward. The Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen took RE-source into its collection, which the organizer calls rare for a research project.

CLEVER°FRANKE designed the visual identity of the 2020 Eurovision Song Contest in Rotterdam, called Open Up, a series of bright vectors radiating from the center of a circle, with colors from the flags of 41 participating countries.
Marjan van Aubel, whom the organizer calls the 2019 Public Award winner, designed a solar roof of light, recyclable PET panels for the Dutch pavilion at the World Expo in Dubai, planned for 2021.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagreed, and what settled it

r: Eight winners (the pre-vote update, and the 2019 rules, which say the public votes on winners from the categories) or all 24 (the results update). A nominee won, so I conclude that all 24 were votable, which the rules as written do not describe. I cannot reconcile the rule with the result.
Fashion nominee and Young Designer nominee, both in the archive.
Not stated in the photographs; stated by the organizer's results update.
In 2019 the entry texts are committee statements; the jury is the eight committee chairs.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know where the Award Night was held, how many submissions the 36 committee members reviewed, or the vote count beyond more than 5,000.
I did not verify the photo-based statements in this pass. Nothing here describes what the Dutch Design Awards 2026 will show.
If a public vote lets a nominee beat the jury's winners, which of the two judgments would you want an award to protect, and which would you want it to question?

posts.title: The Dutch Design Awards 2020 were announced one category per afternoon on a festival television channel, with no hall, no Public Award and an exhibition put off to 2021
posts.subtitle: The 2020 awards read through the organizer's updates and committee statements, the festival's pandemic releases, the entry pages and the official photo archive
posts.seoTitle: Dutch Design Awards 2020: eight afternoons on DDW TV
posts.description: How the 2020 Dutch Design Awards were presented online during the pandemic, who won in each category, what the committees wrote, and what the record does not show.

r: The Dutch Design Awards of 2020 had no ceremony hall: the organizer announced one category per afternoon for eight days on the festival's own television channel, and the physical exhibition was put off to a date in 2021.

I like an award that can be checked against its own paperwork. This essay reads the 2020 awards from public sources only: the organizer's updates and its committee statements, the festival's releases during the pandemic, the entry pages and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive. It reports no visit and no interview, and where sources disagree it says which one settled the question.

blocks.x: Planning around a pandemic

r: The call for entries was extended to May 25 because of the coronavirus, the festival announced.
The organizer later said it closed two months later than planned, and that the Award Night would be held online and the exhibition moved to a date to be set in 2021.
In its words, a Dutch Design Week with more than 350,000 visitors was not realistic.

The live festival did not survive either. On September 30, 2020 the mayor of Eindhoven decided, on advice from the Safety Region, that the live Dutch Design Week could not take place, and the festival became a virtual one.

The closing release says the organization was told two weeks before the start, then built a virtual festival with more than 1,500 designers and 750 3D Viewing Rooms that stayed online for ninety days instead of nine, and claims a reach of several hundred thousand, mainly professionals.
That reach is the organizer's own estimate, and I found no audited count.
The 2020 awards list 24 nominations, three in each of eight categories: Product, Habitat, Communication, Fashion, Design Research, Service & Systems, Best Commissioning and Young Designer.

Eight chairs led 34 design experts in choosing the nominations from all submitted and scouted projects: Angelique Spaninks for Design Research, Bert Hagendoorn for Service & Systems, JaapJan Berg for Habitat, Joost Alferink for Product, Liesbeth in 't Hout for Fashion, Pieter Aarts for Best Commissioning, Sonja Haller for Communication and Saskia van Stein for Young Designer.
The criteria were impact, distinctive character, expressiveness and production method, plus some category-specific ones.
The festival's call for 2021 describes that year as the 19th edition, which makes 2020 the 18th by count.

The organizer's PDF names the members behind each chair. Product: Ingeborg van Lieshout, Lonny van Ryswyck, Cees van Dok and Chris Kabel. Communication: Remco van Bladel, Vanessa van Dam, Karin van den Brandt and Joel Galvez. Fashion: Milou van Rossum, Iris Ruisch, Rachid Naas and Branko Popovic. Design Research: Tanja Koning, Daniëlle Arets, Jop Japenga and Eric Klarenbeek. Habitat: Carolien Ligtenberg, Cees van der Veeken, Ellen van der Wal and Jan Nauta. Service & Systems: Shay Raviv, Daniel Sytsma, Liza Enebeis and Bas van de Poel. Best Commissioning: Madeleine van Lennep, Luuk Ros, Mark van Iterson, Henk Haaima and Jaina Padberg-Bührmann. Young Designer: Jeroen Junte, Georgette Koning, Thomas Clever, Evelien Reich and Tamar Shafrir.
The jury that picked the winners was chaired by Ine Frings and made up of the chairs, with Ingeborg van Lieshout standing in for Product.

The committee statements are a primary source in their own right: the organizer's PDF names the members of every committee, for example Chris Kabel, Lonny van Ryswyck, Cees van Dok and Ingeborg van Lieshout with Alferink for Product.

blocks.x: The rulebook

r: The organizer's rules for 2020, published in Dutch as a regulation, are a rare primary source for how the awards work. Entry is open to designers, studios, commissioners and producers established or trained in the Netherlands, or established abroad with a Dutch identity; a joint entry counts as one.
Entries cost 75 euros plus VAT in the six main categories and 150 euros plus VAT for Best Commissioning.
The work had to be produced, realized, presented or published between May 1, 2019 and May 1, 2020.

There were two routes in. Committees scouted work in February and March 2020, and designers could also enter themselves between February 20 and March 25, a window the festival later extended to May 25 because of the coronavirus.
The committees, of at least four people each with a chair, drew up a shortlist, judged it on a committee day and set three nominees per category.
On the jury day the chairs of the eight categories discussed the 24 nominees and chose one winner per category together.
A copywriter takes part throughout to write the nomination statements and the jury report, the report is public, and decisions are binding and cannot be argued about by letter.

The criteria in the rules are the four named in the announcements: impact, distinctive character, expressiveness and method of production, with extra criteria for Design Research (a research question with evident potential for the future and exemplary work), Service & Systems (creativity and originality, and technology applied successfully and user-friendly), Young Designer (potential for the future, and work that questions the current state of the discipline) and Best Commissioning (the quality of the brief, strategic impact and durability of the collaboration, innovation in the form of collaboration and professionalism of the parties).
The Young Designer Award excludes students.
On the public prize the rules say it goes to the winner with the most public votes, cast during Dutch Design Week among the winners of the categories.
The Piet Zwart prize is awarded every two years by the professional association of designers, does not accept entries, and is a prize for a body of work.

blocks.x: Eight afternoons on DDW TV

r: The organizer scheduled the announcements on Dutch Design Week's new television studio, DDW TV, as a talk show hosted by Isolde Hallensleben, each afternoon at 16:00 on ddw.nl from October 17 to 24, one category at a time, with the three nominees discussed before the winner was named.

The order was Young Designer on Saturday, October 17; Design Research on Sunday, October 18; Service & Systems on Monday, October 19; Habitat on Tuesday, October 20; Fashion on Wednesday, October 21; Communication on Thursday, October 22; Product on Friday, October 23; and Best Commissioning on Saturday, October 24.
The winners release is dated October 24, the day of the last show.

The jury report was presented on video by project leader Frederiek Dijkstra, and it carries the headline message of the year: designers' capacity for change is accelerating, they turn the drive to improve our living world into concrete action, and the combination of digital and physical is no longer separable from design.
The winners release adds that the jury saw a remarkable amount of own initiative, concepts stripped to the essence, and a growing focus on ethics and meaning.

The awards themselves and the visual identity were designed by George & Harrison, whose creative director Martijn Maas described the starting points as no-nonsense, monumental and a touch of magic, and S.T.R.S. produced them, experimenting with materials and colors.
The organizer's winners item says the 24 designers and studios also had virtual exhibitions.

blocks.x: The eight winners

r: Young Designer went to Simon Dogger. The entry says he works from the perspective of a non-visual designer and looks for more inclusive forms of communication.

The jury said he reminds the design world of its limits, asking how inclusive a design can be for a reality the designer does not know, and that he uses facial recognition technology ingeniously for something positive.
He received the 12,000 euro Keep an Eye Young Designer Grant, and each other nominee 9,000 euros.

Design Research went to Matilde Boelhouwer for Insectology: Food for Buzz, a series of ever-flowering artificial flowers for the five main pollinator groups, built with scientists as emergency food for insects in urban places where nothing grows.
The jury noted that the insects, not the designer, are in the spotlight.

Service & Systems went to MONNIE by Afdeling Buitengewone Zaken and Garage2020, an app developed with Albeda in Rotterdam to help young people with debt pay their bills and reduce arrears, which also makes creditors jointly responsible.
The entry says fifteen percent of young people have a debt.
The jury praised the concept, the name and the impact but wrote that the app's appearance deserves a serious upgrade, an unusual caveat in a winner's text.
Habitat went to Forum Groningen by NL Architects with deMunnik-deJong-Steinhauser, a cultural building on the Grote Markt that the entry calls a life-sized search engine.
The jury called its fit with the historic center courageous and noted the effects of the economic crisis and strict earthquake standards.
NL Architects had won Habitat in 2017 with DeFlat Kleiburg.
Fashion went to Ninamounah for Collection 005 Complete Metamorphosis PT.2, a collection mixing animal and techno-future traits.
The jury said the team presents a more mature image without losing its identity and noted the inclusive catwalk.
Ninamounah had been a 2019 Fashion and Young Designer nominee.

Communication went to Studio Dumbar for DEMO, the Design in Motion Festival, which in 2019 showed motion design on all 80 digital screens of Amsterdam Central Station for 24 hours with 237 designers from 37 countries, curated with Koos Breen and Xavier Monney and made with Exterion Media.
The jury called it a powerful debut and wanted a second edition.

Product went to The Interceptor by The Ocean Cleanup with Fabrique, a solar-powered, internet-connected collector that takes plastic out of rivers, since about 80 percent of the plastic in the oceans comes from rivers, per the entry.
The text calls it a courageous example of the problem-solving capabilities of design.
Fabrique had won Service & Systems in 2015 and Best Commissioning in 2018 with museum projects.

Best Commissioning went to the Dutch national government, the Rijksoverheid, for Water as Leverage for Resilient Cities Asia, a program that designs climate-adaptive concepts for Semarang in Indonesia, Chennai in India and Khulna in Bangladesh.
The jury said it takes the Netherlands to the international level and treats global problems as opportunities.
A water-sector report says it started as a competition to challenge design teams to propose integrated plans for those three cities.

blocks.x: The nominees, and what the committees asked of them

r: The committee statements are candid. For Redesigning Psychiatry by Reframing Studio the committee wrote that aesthetic quality lags somewhat behind the substantive ambition, perhaps by choice, in order to reach several audiences.
Reframing Studio had been a Design Research nominee in 2015 for Project Network.
For RETREAT by Xandra van der Eijk, who scanned parts of a retreating Swiss glacier by hand, the committee wrote that emotion is used as a research tool and a ritual of farewell for ecological grief.

In Communication the other nominees were ENTER ENTER, a non-profit project space in Amsterdam for the art of the book, and Bart de Baets's campaign for the Sandberg Institute master course Radical Cut Up.

In Fashion, Schueller de Waal's Litter sent fifty models in cleaning uniforms made from waste to clean a street in Paris during haute couture week, and Passama/Langendijk made a fur-free collection that researches what fur symbolizes.
Schueller de Waal had won Fashion in 2018.
The Fashion committee called the Litter intervention awareness with impact without compromises on form, and called the fur research an unusual blend of jewelry, fashion and materials.

In Habitat, Studio Ossidiana's Paper Gardens was a scenography for the 2019 Salone del Mobile in Milan, commissioned by The New York Times Style Magazine, and Korthtielens' transformation of the 1970s pavilion school De Molenwiek in Haarlem was done in collaboration with its teachers.
The Habitat committee wrote of Paper Gardens that it looks as if it was made for Instagram but that appearances can deceive, and of the Forum that it is a wonderful gift to the city.

In Product, Auping Evolve is described as the first entirely circular mattress, held together by a bonding system that can be reversed by heat, and The Object Is Absent was an exhibition project by four curators.

In Service & Systems, Thijs Biersteker's Pollutive Ends pumps fifty liters of water a day through pipes to show what one cigarette butt does to water, and Moniker's Repeat After Me gathered visitors' non-verbal voices into one voice in Berlin.
Biersteker returns in 2023 as a Data & Interaction nominee.
In Best Commissioning the other nominees were the municipality of Groningen with NL Architects for the Forum, and Triodos Bank for its De Reehorst office.

The Service & Systems committee, in the document that preceded the jury's choice, was frank about the winner: it deducted points for the graphic design and aesthetics of MONNIE and called its holistic approach what makes it special.
The jury kept that criticism in its own text while crowning the app.
The committee called Pollutive Ends something that makes you think twice before dropping a cigarette butt, and called Repeat After Me pure poetry about our relationship with machines.

The Young Designer nominees were Katinka Versendaal, whose studio The Eatelier works on what she calls speculative gastronomy, and Iris van Wees, who presents digital fashion as an alternative to the current fashion system.

A later organizer update on how the three planned to use the Keep an Eye money says Dogger drew up a spending plan for office equipment, a research project on haptic aesthetics and podcasts about innovation, design and inclusion; Van Wees wrote of better equipment for her digital fashion work; and Versendaal described business coaching and a new website.

blocks.x: What the photographs add

r: The one 2020 album I read on October 9, 2026, and did not reopen for this version, holds 20 photographs of the Habitat afternoon.
The program shows when the Habitat show aired: Tuesday, October 20, in the afternoon.

The photographs show a large industrial hall lit in red, a long wooden table under a screen with the awards' diamond logo, cameras, a few guests and a host, with screens used as captions that name the winner and quote the jury.

blocks.x: Where 2020 sits in the archive, and what happened to MONNIE

r: The organizer's archive lists 24 entries for 2020, the same as every year from 2018.
The count is mine, from the listing.

Studio Dumbar, the Communication winner, has the longest record in this series: it won in 2003 for the TPG Post identity, was nominated in 2004, 2005, 2006, 2010 and 2013, received the Piet Zwart prize in 2009 and won again with DEMO.
Moniker, a Service & Systems nominee for Repeat After Me, had won in 2013 and 2018.
Fabrique's Interceptor win followed Service & Systems in 2015 and Best Commissioning in 2018.
The Ocean Cleanup itself was a Best Commissioning nominee in 2021.
Two nominees had earlier links. Barbara Langendijk, half of Passama/Langendijk, had been a Young Designer finalist in 2015.
Bart de Baets had been a Product nominee in 2012.
Royal Auping, behind Auping Evolve, had been a Best Commissioning nominee in 2011.
The jury's one criticism of a winner has an answer in the record. The MONNIE jury wrote that the app's appearance deserves a serious upgrade.

A later organizer video page says the app announced a name change shortly after filming, going on as Seev under the motto Better Seev than sorry, and that since winning the award it has also received a new visual identity.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagreed, and what settled it

r: The organizer's news item is dated October 20, and the schedule confirms Tuesday, October 20.
Whether there was a Public Award.
The 2020 pages I read mention none, and the physical exhibition was postponed.
I name no 2020 Public Award winner.
The Forum Groningen appears twice: as the Habitat winner and, with the municipality named as the commissioning party, as a Best Commissioning nominee.
The product entry shows committee wording; the others show a jury paragraph.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know whether the postponed exhibition took place in 2021, or where, because I found no page that says so.
I do not know how many submissions the committees reviewed, or who built the studio set for the shows.
I did not verify the photo-based statements in this pass. Nothing here describes what the Dutch Design Awards 2026 will show.
If an award can be given to a camera, which part of a prize survives the loss of the room, and which part was never about the room at all?

posts.title: The Dutch Design Awards 2022 gave eight prizes, four partner awards and a public vote to a project about care, and a new jury chair asked who was in the room
posts.subtitle: The 2022 awards read through the organizer's updates, jury report and entry pages, the festival's releases, a university study on the selection process and the official photo archive
posts.seoTitle: Dutch Design Awards 2022: winners, partner awards, public vote
posts.description: Who won the Dutch Design Awards in 2022, what the juries wrote, how four partner awards and a public vote worked, and what a study of the selection process found.

r: The Dutch Design Awards of 2022 gave eight category prizes, four partner awards and a public vote that went to Kleinkijkacademie, a project that turned everyday care tasks into an experience for the people who give care.

I like an award that can be checked against its own paperwork. This essay reads the 2022 awards from public sources only: the organizer's updates, jury report and entry pages, the festival's releases, a university study of the selection process and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive. It reports no visit and no interview, and where sources disagree it says which one settled the question.

blocks.x: A new jury chair, and the structure behind eight prizes

r: The nominees were announced in early July: expert juries nominated three projects in each of eight categories, Product, Habitat, Communication, Fashion, Design Research, Data & Interaction, Best Commissioning and Young Designer.
Data & Interaction, which had already replaced Service & Systems in the 2021 call for entries, was a category again.

The update names the chairs of the expert juries: Chris Kabel, JaapJan Berg, Mieke Gerritzen, Iris Ruisch, Angelique Spaninks, Daniel Sytsma, Tijn van Elderen of Brabantia and Evelien Reich of ELLE Decoration, who judged on impact, distinctive character, expressiveness and production method, sometimes with category-specific criteria.

The update lists them in the same order as the categories; I read them as Product, Habitat, Communication, Fashion, Design Research, Data & Interaction, Best Commissioning and Young Designer. A 2023 update in which the chairs talk about their categories confirms the pairings for Design Research, Communication, Young Designer, Product, Best Commissioning and Data & Interaction, and the 2023 winners item lists the same people with two stand-ins.

Tijn van Elderen is a name worth pausing on. The 2016 entry for the Best Client Award winner Brabantia names its CEO as Tijn van Elderen, and in 2022 an update lists a Tijn van Elderen of Brabantia as a jury chair.
The pages do not say they are the same person. The match is close, and the company is the same.
The main jury had a new chair that year, Kevin de Randamie, whom the organizer introduces as a hip-hop artist known as Blaxtar and the founder of Cre8tive Revolution.

He told the organizer the process was professionally organized, that there was room for every perspective even though the main jury was still a relatively homogeneous group, and that the expert juries and entries were far more pluralistic.
He also said he associated design earlier with aesthetics and now sees much more design thinking, with reverence for purpose in the room.

blocks.x: Who judged

r: The organizer's 2022 booklet names each expert jury with affiliations. Product: Chris Kabel (chair), Amanda Pinatih of the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam, Kristina Andersen of Eindhoven University of Technology, Floris Schoonderbeek and Cees van Dok of Miro. Habitat: JaapJan Berg (chair) of Bergplaats, Ellen van der Wal, Femke Bijlsma, Cees van der Veeken and Jan Nauta. Communication: Mieke Gerritzen (chair) of The Image Society, Thecla Schaeffer, Karen van de Kraats, Bas Koopmans and René Toneman. Fashion: Iris Ruisch (chair) of State of Fashion, Marga Weimans, Branko Popovic, Rachid Naas and Mehtap Gungormez.

Design Research: Angelique Spaninks (chair) of MU Hybrid Art House, Michelle Kasprzak, Danielle Arets, Jop Japenga and Eric Klarenbeek. Data & Interaction: Daniel Sytsma (chair) of Dentsu Creative, Liza Enebeis of Studio Dumbar, Merel van Helsdingen of Nxt Museum, Bas van der Poel of Modem and Shay Raviv. Best Commissioning: Tijn van Elderen (chair) of Brabantia, Madeleine van Lennep of BNO, Jaina Padberg-Bührmann of Coolblue, Milou Pikaart of HEMA, Eelco van Collenburg of Valtech and Rinske Jurgens of the Textielmuseum. Young Designer: Evelien Reich (chair) of ELLE Decoration NL, Aynouk Tan, Liv Vaisberg, Gabrielle Kennedy of DAMN° Magazine, Thomas Clever of CLEVER°FRANKE and Borre Akkersdijk of BYBORRE.

The panels mix curators, journalists, educators and practitioners from firms that appear elsewhere in the archive. Studio Dumbar won Communication in 2020, Modem won it in 2023 and CLEVER°FRANKE won Data & Interaction in 2021 and 2023, and each had a person on a 2022 jury.

Those are separate years and categories. I read this as a sign of how small and interlinked the field is, and it says nothing about any decision. The study of the selection process, described below, was commissioned by the same organizer.

blocks.x: An outside view

r: The booklet also commissions an outside reading. Nick Axel of e-flux Architecture, who also heads the architectural design department at the Gerrit Rietveld Academie, writes under the title Living the Dream that the nominees offer good ideas and beautiful things but also sincerity, engagement and praxis.

He quotes the point that identifying a problem does not mean knowing the solution, and uses Kleinkijkacademie to argue that sometimes what is needed is a process that helps understand the problem better.
He calls the Depot Boijmans Van Beuningen a beacon showing what the future of museums looks like.

blocks.x: What the jury report said about the year

r: The jury report names relevance to society, collaboration and critical reflection as the marks of the winners, and says the heart speaks as much as the head: projects appeal to emotion and push toward change, not only awareness.
It describes a shift from treating symptoms to changing systems, a more visible role for female designers, many community-driven projects and a stronger educational component.
It calls modesty a refreshing trend, with the solo designer largely replaced by collaboration, and notes that circular design has become the new baseline.
The report also names costs. Since the previous year designers faced scarcity of people, raw materials and expertise, which pushed them to become material developers.
It raises a question for the next year, whether the no-data-collection movement will appear among the entries.
And it notes that high design quality is not yet a given outcome of design thinking now used strategically in more sectors.

The winners release, in the festival's English version, says the winners respond to societal challenges and are full of heart, with the younger designers giving strikingly clear perspectives on urgent social themes.

blocks.x: October 27 and the eight winners

r: The winners were announced and celebrated on October 27, 2022, at the DDA Award Night during Dutch Design Week, which ran October 22 to 30.
All nominated and winning projects were shown in the nine-day exhibition in Microlab Hall.

Data & Interaction went to Studio Noa Jansma for BUYCLOUD, a video installation linked to a speculative market and online land registry that sells clouds, drawing parallels between colonialism, climate change and extraterrestrial occupation.
The jury called it light-footed and razor sharp, noted that the young Jansma initiated the project herself, and read it as a subtle indictment of the NFT game.

The nominee list for the same category included Random Studio's Erode, which applies erosion to NFTs, and Superposition's data visualization for Amnesty International on facial recognition in New York.
Communication went to CAPS LOCK, a book by Ruben Pater published by Valiz on how capitalism and graphic design are linked, with six radical design initiatives as counterpoints.
The jury called it the life's work of a designer who is obsessed with his field and said it becomes compulsory reading for design students.
The nominees were WeTransfer's Traces with Marina Abramovic and Merijn and Jurriaan Hos's campaign film for Down the Rabbit Hole.

Design Research went to Studio Makkink & Bey for the IABR Down to Earth Waterschool M4H+, researched with forty designers for the 6,300 future inhabitants of Merwe-Vierhavens in Rotterdam, around five resources: insects, duckweed, seaweed, wood and fungi.
The jury called it a textbook example of how design research can play an educational role.
The studio was a Product finalist in 2015 with the PROOFFLab Magazine, and its two founders were that year's festival ambassadors.

Fashion went to Yamuna Forzani for The Utopia Ball x Fashion Show, a ballroom competition with a fashion show that has grown into a platform for young designers in the Dutch ballroom scene, which the entry describes as a community by and for trans people of color and non-binary and queer people of color.
The jury called it empowering and a third space for people excluded elsewhere.
The Fashion nominees were Studio David Laport and Antoine Peters.

Habitat went to MVRDV for Depot Boijmans Van Beuningen, the world's first publicly accessible art depot, holding 151,000 works over 14 depot spaces in a round building with a reflective facade and a roof garden.
The jury called it an iconic building and a new typology for what a depot can be.

The museum's own page says the depot was opened on November 5, 2021 by King Willem-Alexander, holds fourteen climate-controlled compartments, and that visitors see the works arranged by climate need and not by period.

The entry says 151,000 artworks, while the museum's page says more than 152,000 artworks from the museum and from private and corporate collections, out of a museum collection of more than 154,000 objects.

The figures differ because they count different things on different dates; I use the entry's number only where I quote the entry. MVRDV had met the public vote before, when Crystal Houses won it in 2016.
The Habitat nominees were the 45 meter wooden residential building Stories in Amsterdam and the VisKringloop spawning ground in the Wieringermeer.
Product went to REX, the first Dutch chair with a deposit, designed by Ineke Hans in 2011 and re-released by Circuform as a recyclable chair that can be returned for a guaranteed 20 euro deposit.
The jury said it does away with furniture as a disposable item and creates an ecosystem that gives value to exchangeable furniture.
The Product nominees were Buro Belen's Sun+ Shadecloth and Sabine Marcelis's Mirage.
Best Commissioning went to the Victim Support Fund and Morrow for WTFFF!?, an interactive platform for young people about online sexual abuse, told in the young people's own words.
The entry reports that more than a hundred thousand children and young people in the Netherlands face such abuse each year.
The jury praised the commissioning body for staying in the background, and the production quality from sound design to motion graphics.
The other nominees were Fabrique's work for Service Apotheek and Vlisco's Fest of Movement, a mural designed by Simone Post for the company's 175th anniversary.

Young Designer went to Cream on Chrome, the Rotterdam duo Martina Huynh and Jonas Althaus, who graduated from the Design Academy Eindhoven in 2018 and make design research and interactive installations such as the Basic Income Cafe, which Huynh had shown as a 2019 Design Research nominee.
The jury said we will keep seeing them for years.

The nominees were Irene Ha, whose Baby Reni brand represents identities of the (South-East) Asian diaspora and which the committee describes as owned, built and sold together with her community, and Leo Maher, who graduated cum laude with a project on the history of homosexuality and its material culture.

blocks.x: More on the nominees

r: The committee texts say why each nominee was on the list. In Data & Interaction, Superposition's work for Amnesty International let users map a walking route through New York City and see where facial recognition surveillance may reach them, and the committee said it makes lengthy research reports comprehensible and concrete.
The committee for Erode wrote that when you use a physical product it erodes, and that Random Studio applied that principle to digital artworks.

In Communication, WeTransfer's WePresent platform asked Marina Abramovic to choose five items to preserve for future generations, among them a stone from Mars and Van Gogh's Starry Night, and the committee admired WeTransfer for building its brand through an art platform.
The Down the Rabbit Hole film took the weight of the world as its starting point, and the committee said it shows a festival identity transcending itself.

In Design Research, Studio Zsofia Kollar's Human Material Loop turns hair, which the project text says amounts to around 72 million kilograms of waste a year in Europe alone, into a biomaterial, shown as a sweater.

In Fashion, Studio David Laport's Local Vegetation is the studio's tenth collection, and the committee read the pandemic setbacks as a push toward a new working method; Antoine Peters's Space Garments in the Bonnefanten Museum turned sleeves and jeans into a landscape visitors could enter.

In Habitat, Stories is a 45 meter high wooden residential building in Amsterdam-Noord built largely with bio-based materials as a self-build project, and VisKringloop is a spawning and breeding ground for fish in the Wieringermeer polder.

In Product, Buro Belen's Sun+ lets in the UV rays the body needs for vitamin D instead of blocking all of them, and Sabine Marcelis's Mirage combines reflective and sandblasted glass in a piece commissioned by the Collectional Gallery in Dubai.
In Best Commissioning, Service Apotheek asked Fabrique to think about its service in a world of fast delivery, and the committee called the result a crash course in commissioning.
Fabrique had won Best Commissioning in 2018 with the museum project Het Grootste Museum van Nederland.

Vlisco turned its concrete head office into a celebration of color for its 175th anniversary with an intervention by Simone Post, who had won Young Designer in 2019 and whose Post-Vlisco carpet was a 2016 finalist.

blocks.x: Four partner awards and a public vote

r: The organizer presented four additional awards through partners. The Keep an Eye Foundation gave the Young Designer winner 12,000 euros and each of the two other nominees, Irene Ha and Leo Maher, 9,000 euros.
For the DDA x MINI Award, MINI chose Buro Belen from all 24 nominees, with a year in a special-edition electric MINI.
The DDA x EY Award, a coaching program, went to Cream on Chrome.
The first DDA x Catawiki Award, with a cash prize, a photo shoot and a feature on Catawiki's auction site, also went to Buro Belen.
The Public Award went to Kleinkijkacademie by Sjaak Langenberg and Rose de Beer, announced at the Award Night.

The entry describes designers and artists who transformed everyday care tasks into experiences for residents with severe mental or multiple disabilities, on behalf of the care organization Severinus, giving their supervisors new insights.
The committee wrote that the designers found a profound yet light-hearted way to ease care tasks and that they make the invisible tangible.
I name no resident and no detail of a person's care. The vote count is not given.
Cream on Chrome said a year later that winning gave them breathing room to ask what their projects have in common, and a sense of having landed in the design community.

blocks.x: A study of who gets chosen

r: The Dutch Design Foundation worked in 2022 with the Rotterdam School of Management at Erasmus University on a study of the selection and assessment process, to see whether ideas by women and ethnic minorities are judged more strictly and whether novelty affects the judgment.
The lead researcher is Dirk Deichmann.

The first findings, reported by the organizer, looked at entries from 2019 and 2020 and found no support for the theory that novel entries by women are punished more, and gender did not seem to affect who reached the shortlist or a nomination.
Deichmann called some results hopeful signals but possibly a one-off, said the study continues, and listed follow-ups such as the culture of the submitter.
The study looks at gender and ethnicity in the entry data. It cannot say anything about the 2022 results, and it is early.

blocks.x: A festival that matched a peak year

r: The festival's closing release says DDW22, under the theme Get Set, We're on a mission, was on the level of peak year 2019 in visitor numbers, without giving a figure, and names Andrea Trimarchi and Simone Farresin of Formafantasma as ambassadors.
The program release lists seven thematic exhibitions in the Klokgebouw and on Ketelhuisplein and a RetroFuture exhibition in the Evoluon.

blocks.x: What the exhibition photographs add

r: The Microlab Hall album, which I read on October 9, 2026 and did not reopen for this version, shows a white-floored hall with steel pillars, tall black frames and gray leaning boards, with a ballot box marked Stem hier, Vote here, and a board for the Communication winner with a line from the book.

blocks.x: Where 2022 sits in the archive

r: The organizer's archive lists 24 entries for 2022, the same size as every year since 2018.
The count is mine, from the listing.
Random Studio had been a 2021 Communication nominee before its 2022 and 2023 Data & Interaction nominations, which makes it the only studio in the list with three straight years.
Fabrique's name appears in the archive in eleven different years between 2003 and 2022 by my count, the last being the Service Apotheek nomination.
MVRDV's Habitat win came after nominations in 2010, 2015 and 2017 and the 2016 public win.
Studio Makkink & Bey's win followed its 2015 nomination.
Vlisco's name is on the archive through Post-Vlisco Carpet in 2016, Vlisco un a un in 2017 and Fest of Movement in 2022.
Sabine Marcelis, whose Mirage was a Product finalist, had been named an ambassador of Dutch Design Week for the 2020 edition, IO+ reported in 2019.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagreed, and what settled it

r: The Dutch version of the winners item prints Cream on Chrome in one place under Best Commissioning, while the English version and the archive put it under Young Designer. The Young Designer grant and the entry page settle it.
When the Utopia Ball took place.
The entry says the 2021 ball was held at the Kunsthal in Rotterdam as part of Rotterdam Pride. I could not open a Kunsthal page to check the month, so I repeat the entry's words and no date.
The winners item credits Ruben Pater; the nominee list credits Valiz. The entry says Valiz published the book written and designed by Pater, so both are right.
151,000 (entry), more than 152,000 in the depot and more than 154,000 in the collection (museum). I give each with its source.
Whether the new chair of Best Commissioning is the 2016 Brabantia CEO.
Same name and company in two documents. I say the match is close and unconfirmed.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know the Public Award's vote count, the number of submissions, or the total visitors of DDW22.
I did not verify the photo-based statements in this pass. Nothing here describes what the Dutch Design Awards 2026 will show.
If a jury chair says the room was still homogeneous while the entries were not, which of the two should an award change first?

posts.title: The Dutch Design Awards 2023 were decided in September, shown in October, and the public chose a walking forest, before the awards took a year to reflect
posts.subtitle: The 2023 awards read through the organizer's updates and entry pages, the festival's releases, the chairs' own words and the official photo archive
posts.seoTitle: Dutch Design Awards 2023: winners, public vote, then a pause
posts.description: Who won the Dutch Design Awards in 2023, how the public vote went to Bosk, what the expert panels asked of the nominees, and why 2024 became a year of reflection.

r: The Dutch Design Awards of 2023 named their winners in September, showed them in October, let visitors choose by scanning a QR code, and the visitors chose Bosk, a walking forest of more than a thousand trees that had already won Habitat.

I like an award that can be checked against its own paperwork. This essay reads the 2023 awards from public sources only: the organizer's updates and entry pages, the festival's releases, the chairs' own words and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive. It reports no visit and no interview, and where sources disagree it says which one settled the question.

blocks.x: Thursday, September 21, and a main jury that kept asking about categories

r: The festival's winners item says the eight winners were presented on Thursday, September 21, 2023, at the festive DDA Award Night, and that all winning and nominated entries would be shown at the DDA23 exhibition during Dutch Design Week, October 21 to 29.

Under the supervision of main jury chair Dymphie Braun, the winners were selected by the chairs of the expert juries: Chris Kabel, Femke Bijlsma, Mieke Gerritzen, Iris Ruisch, Daniëlle Arets for Angelique Spaninks, Merel van Helsdingen for Daniël Sytsma, Tijn van Elderen and Evelien Reich.
Arets and Van Helsdingen stood in on an interim basis.

The 2023 winners item makes an observation that explains the year. The expert juries assessed more projects than ever that would not have looked out of place in another category, so the question arises whether design can still be categorized the same way.

Most submissions were crossovers, and next to makership, research and collaboration the underlying themes were the personal as a starting point, a wide range of perspectives and the need for meaning and connection.

In a series of Instagram Live conversations, the chairs described their categories. Angelique Spaninks said Design Research does not always yield tangible products but gives form to research, formulates questions or starts collaborations.
Mieke Gerritzen said Communication is broadening away from graphic design toward human connection with design.
Evelien Reich noticed a shift in Young Designer from mission-driven to more personal work, and said the winner's international perspective challenges the notion of Dutch in Dutch Design Awards.
Chris Kabel acknowledged the many international entries and stressed the flourishing talent in the Netherlands.
Tijn van Elderen stressed that good commissioning takes long-term collaboration, time, space and trust.
Daniel Sytsma said Data & Interaction recognizes organizations that share data as well as designers.

Femke Bijlsma underlined the breadth of Habitat, which covers architecture, urban planning, landscape and interior design, and Iris Ruisch said Fashion has shifted from a product focus to process-oriented, socially aware practice.
By the count of the festival's 2021 call, which names that year the 19th edition, 2023 was the 21st.
The 2017 announcement says the awards date from 2003.
I could not find a 2023 page that states the edition number, so the 21st is an inference from the count.

blocks.x: The eight winners

r: Data & Interaction went to CLEVER°FRANKE for Voices from the Frontlines, a website and report for the Global Centre for Climate Mobility that turns two years of research into stories about climate-driven displacement in Africa, with the entry citing an estimate of up to 113 million people moving by 2050.

The panel called the agency a master at visualizing and opening up complex data, and said the work makes visible the impact on places that often go unnoticed by policymakers, news media and the public, in portions politicians and journalists can work with.
The firm had been a finalist in 2015 and a winner in 2019.
Communication went to Modem for the Modem Research Papers, a series on the impact of digitization, made with independent artists, writers, studios and universities and shared freely.

The panel praised their attractive, accessible presentation, which it said research agencies rarely show, and noted that it also showcases the agency's strengths to potential commissioners by translating research into new forms of communication.

Design Research went to Studio Carlijn Kingma for The Waterworks of Our Money, in which the cartographer Carlijn Kingma, with the financial economists Thomas Bollen and Martijn van der Linden, explains the monetary system through water metaphors and architectural illustrations.
The panel noted workshops at banks and the collaboration with the platform Follow the Money, and said the smart animations based on the illustrations bring the subjects to life.

Fashion went to Tailors and Wearers, a platform for Afro-Surinamese fashion and heritage that publishes, teaches and exhibits, including a book called Goma Weri and an exhibition about the angisa headscarf.
The panel said it initiates a relevant change of course in Dutch fashion, and named modern interpretations by young designers such as Denzel Veerkamp.

Habitat went to Bosk, by Arcadia, the municipality of Leeuwarden and Bruno Doedens, a walking forest of more than a thousand trees that took over the center of Leeuwarden for a hundred days in summer 2022, moved repeatedly by residents over 3.5 kilometers with 4,000 volunteers.

The municipality's own page dates the walk to May 7 through August 14, 2022, and credits the idea to the late Joop Mulder of Sense of Place and the concept to Bruno Doedens in collaboration with Arcadia, the 100-day cultural program that followed Leeuwarden's year as European Capital of Culture.

The panel noted that the municipality committed in advance to give the trees a permanent home, called the project gentle yet firm pressure to make cities greener, and asked in which other cities Bosk should appear next.

After August 14 the trees and thousands of seedlings were given permanent places in Leeuwarden and Friesland, the municipality says, with locations listed including two industrial estates and sites where ash dieback had killed trees.
The jury line on the entry page says that when the forest moves on, it is missed, and a follow-up piece a year later repeats the panel's praise.

Product went to Super Local for From the Himalayas, which turns water bottle caps carried back from Sagarmatha National Park in Nepal into pebble-shaped souvenirs, with the proceeds financing the workshop.
The panel said the bags are both functional and a signal to fellow climbers, and that it would like to see the system at festivals and diving spots.
Super Local had been a Young Designer finalist in 2017.
Best Commissioning went to Rotterdam Circulair with Christien Meindertsma for The Soft City, the municipality's commission to find uses for the wool of 2,500 sheep that graze public green spaces.

The museum's account says Meindertsma began working with wool in 2007, that her research took a key turn in 2020 when Rotterdam Circulair commissioned her, and that Rotterdam's grazing flock yields 5,000 kilograms of virgin wool a year.
The panel's headline was from mess to yes, and it said the commissioner must dare to manage uncertainty, which is not self-evident for a municipality.
Meindertsma had won Product and the Future Award in 2016 with the FLAX Chair.
Young Designer went to Marcos Kueh, who weaves contemporary versions of Borneo's story textiles and works on postcolonial themes, in a decision the panel called unanimous.
Kueh is also one half of the duo Sampat Studio, which was a Product nominee.

The BNO Piet Zwart Prize, from a dedicated jury chaired by Timo de Rijk, went to the graphic designer Karel Martens, whom the jury credited with an extraordinary contribution to the meaning and standing of the field.

blocks.x: The public chose a forest

r: Visitors to the exhibition in Microlab could vote with QR codes placed beside the projects until Thursday, October 26 at 12:00, and the winner was to be announced that evening at interCHANGES, a series of events by the festival.
The festival says the public award went to Bosk, aligning with the jury, and the closing release says Bosk won decisively.

blocks.x: Five themes instead of eight categories

r: The organizer's own booklet says the 2023 exhibition presented nominees and winners under five themes that stood out to the juries: Inquisitive, Makership, Meaning & Connection, Personal & Perspective and Interdisciplinary.
The reason it gives is the one in the winners item, that crossovers make up the majority of entries and that design may no longer be categorized in the old way.

The booklet's index shows how that regrouped the field. CLEVER°FRANKE, Modem and The Soft City sit under Inquisitive, with Biersteker's MB>CO2. Studio Carlijn Kingma's Waterworks sits under Makership, with Simone Post's Candy Land, Sampat Studio's Wayang Kulit and Omlab's swallow homes. Tailors and Wearers and Bosk sit under Meaning & Connection with The New Stijl, the North Sea project, De Kunstwerf and Groenmarkt. Marcos Kueh sits under Personal & Perspective with Missjourney.ai, Dae Uk Kim, HENK, Paul Kooiker and the Atlas of Queer Anatomy. From the Himalayas sits under Interdisciplinary with Random Studio's Gucci fresco, LOADS and Gabriel Fontana.

It also lists the 2023 main jury by category with each chair's affiliation: Chris Kabel for Product, Femke Bijlsma for Habitat, Mieke Gerritzen for Communication, Iris Ruisch for Fashion, Angelique Spaninks for Design Research, Daniel Sytsma for Data & Interaction, Tijn van Elderen of Brabantia for Best Commissioning and Evelien Reich for Young Designer, with Dymphy Braun, described as a cultural producer and curator, as chair.
The booklet spells her first name Dymphy where the festival's English item says Dymphie.

blocks.x: An outside view

r: The booklet commissions an outside reading. Oli Stratford, editor-in-chief of Disegno, opens by confessing that he has never sat on the judging panel, does not live in the Netherlands and is unsure what Dutch design means in a critical sense.

He argues that what makes contemporary Dutch design interesting is its role as a microcosm of the field worldwide, with practitioners who are Dutch by birth, base, training, project or by the support their work receives, and that national identity survives through infrastructure such as education, employment and routes to the public.
He calls the awards an integral engine for driving the field forward.

He singles out two nominees. The Embassy of the North Sea's mock trial at the Peace Palace shows the capacity of design to frame questions of urgent social value, and Simone Post's Candy Land, with window frames of braided marshmallow and chandeliers of candy necklaces, shows delight in materiality and has no explicit social message, which he says is also needed.
He closes that the field is fractured and expansive and that the nominees are moments of partial illumination.

blocks.x: The nominees, and one that I read with a professional eye

r: The expert panels' notes on the nominees read as arguments. Thijs Biersteker's MB>CO2, which turns the carbon cost of your video calls into puffs of smoke, was praised for excelling on concept, design, execution and effect, and he had been a 2020 finalist for Pollutive Ends.
Random Studio's Gucci fresco ran over 33 LED screens in Chengdu with an AI trained on oil paintings, and Random Studio had been a 2022 finalist for Erode.
In Communication, Simone Post's shop windows for Hermès in Tokyo were praised as a dreamy escapism at a time when Japan was still in lockdown, and Post had won Young Designer in 2019.
The New Stijl, from …,STAAT, is a book celebrating a generation of Dutch makers.
In Design Research, the Embassy of the North Sea staged a mock court in the Peace Palace in The Hague to give the sea a voice.

The other nominee in that category, the Atlas of Queer Anatomy by Kuang-Yi Ku and the medical professor Henry de Vries, answers the standard textbook Atlas of Human Anatomy from 1957 and invites young doctors and creatives to add collages to a queer atlas.

As an anatomist, I read this entry with particular interest, because it aims its challenge at how anatomy is taught. The panel wrote that the anatomy is the same but the lens makes you see differently.

In Fashion, Paul Kooiker's solo show at Foam brought fashion images, all shot on an iPhone, into one installation, and Lisa Konno's HENK made a film, a collection and a book about the Surinamese-Dutch caretaker of the Rietveld Academy; Konno had won Young Designer in 2018.

In Habitat, De Kunstwerf gave Groningen's theater companies a purpose-built home, and Groenmarkt in Amsterdam, where the panel noted that the beds of elderly couples in the care homes can be placed next to each other.
In Product, Sampat Studio's Wayang Kulit interweaves the physical and digital, and Omlab's 3D-printed swallow starter homes are described as helping birds until nature recovers.

In Best Commissioning, Studio Claudy Jongstra's self-financed LOADS promotes dye plant cultivation and educational projects, and Missjourney.ai by TEDxAmsterdam Women and ACE is an AI tool designed to counter gender and origin bias.
The Young Designer nominees were Gabriel Fontana, who uses sport as a metaphor for society, and Dae Uk Kim, who reworks objects connected to a hard childhood in Korea.

blocks.x: The festival that held the exhibition

r: The festival's closing release gives the frame: Dutch Design Week 2023 ran under the theme Picture This, with beacons Muzus, Yinka Ilori and Stefan Diez, and it launched interCHANGES, a series of interactive events for mission-driven people that opened with three co-creation sessions.
The release also mentions the Avenue of Fresh Perspectives, an exploration of the newest generation of makers, and PONT, a multi-year collaboration that uses design power for societal challenges.
The Public Award was announced at the third interCHANGES session, which is how the awards plugged into the festival's own new format.

blocks.x: What came after: a year of reflection

r: The organizer announced that in 2024 there would be no regular edition. Dutch Design Awards chose a year of reflection, asking who the awards are for, whom they reach and whom they do not, and what is celebrated.
It would redesign its process with people from different groups and spotlight Young Designers.

The festival's release adds that the awards would work with ten previous winners or nominees from Young Designer, each introducing a promising name, with interviews by Evelien Reich, and a Dutch Design Awards exhibition at Dutch Design Week 2024 built around the festival's five missions.
The archive now carries Emerging Talent Award listings for 2025 and 2026.

The organizer's current pages say the awards continue with a renewed focus on emerging talent, in which established designers nominate exceptional new voices, and that thinking of design through predefined categories no longer reflects the richness of today's design landscape.
The same page says the awards were established in 2003 thanks to BNO and DesignLink.
I describe the later format only through those statements.
A digital booklet of the winning and nominated projects followed, with an outside view of Dutch design by Oli Stratford and a piece on the Piet Zwart winner Karel Martens.
A follow-up series called In Focus revisited the 2023 winners a year later, including Bosk and Modem.

blocks.x: What the exhibition photographs add

r: The Microlab album, which I read on October 9, 2026 and did not reopen for this version, shows boards in a row, each with a category and a status, Winner or Nominee, project text in Dutch and English and a short jury line.
That layout matches the way the organizer's pages are organized online.

blocks.x: Where 2023 sits in the archive

r: The organizer's archive lists 24 entries for 2023, the same size as every year since 2018.
The count is mine, from the listing.
The people who recur are the story of the list. CLEVER°FRANKE is listed in 2013, 2015, 2019, 2021 and 2023, with wins in 2019, 2021 and 2023.
Christien Meindertsma is listed in 2008, 2013, 2016 and 2023 and is spotlighted again in the 2024 listings.
Simone Post is listed in 2016, 2019 and 2023.
Random Studio is listed in 2021, 2022 and 2023.
Thijs Biersteker is listed in 2020 and 2023.
Lisa Konno won in 2018 and was nominated again in 2023.
Super Local was a Young Designer finalist in 2017 and a Product winner in 2023.

Read against the 2023 winners item, the repeat names support its observation about crossovers: designers who started in one category were by 2023 being judged in another, and the committees were asking whether categories still describe the work.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagreed, and what settled it

r: The organizer's winners item lists none, and the festival item and the closing release name Bosk.

The entry says 4,000 volunteers and a total distance of 3.5 kilometers. The municipality says more than 1,000 trees. A news report at the start said 1,200 trees and more than 5,000 volunteers. I give the entry's volunteers and the municipality's trees, because the news report was written as the walk began and describes a forecast.
The Dutch and English winners items spell several project names differently, for example De Zachte Stad and The Soft City. They are the same entries.
Who chaired Design Research and Data & Interaction.
The winners item lists stand-ins for Spaninks and Sytsma; the later chairs' conversation speaks for their categories.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know the vote count, the number of submissions, or where the Award Night was held.
I did not verify the photo-based statements in this pass. Nothing here describes what the Dutch Design Awards 2026 will show.
If an award finds that most of its entries could sit in another category, what is it still measuring?
